full_judgment:
7. On 31-12-88 the Respondent No.2 the land acquisition officer, Dhaka caused a notice served in L.A. Case. No.8/88-89 by virtue of section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 stating that the land mentioned in the schedule to the said notice was required or likely to be required for public purpose for setting up a three-star Hotel. An objection was also invited from the persons interested in the said land, it is submitted that the notice  was not published at convenient places or near the property sought to be acquired as in required under the provision of the Ordinance and as such the petitioners were absolutely in dark about the notice of requisition. Having come to know from the neighbouring people that some portion of the land around Sundarban Hotel was going to be acquired the petitioners went to the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and to their utter surprise and dismey found that the land of the petitioners mentioned in the schedule of the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance along with some other properties were purported to have been requisitioned and acquired. Immediately they met the respondent No. 2 and intimated him that the notice appearing in the board was never published on or near the land. On being advised the petitioners raised objection and produced the documents before the respondent No.2 who after hearing the petitioners and examining the documents of title seemed to have been convinced about the genuineness of the claim of the petitioners in respect of the land in question but did nothing so as to exclude the same from acquisition. In spite of the objections raised the petitioners was served with another notice on 11.2.1989 under section 6 of the Ordinance wherein it was stated that, the Government has decided to acquire the property mentioned in the schedule to the notice for the purpose of setting up a 3-Star Hotel therein. The owners and occupiers of the land were also directed to appear before the respondent No on 28-2-1989 in connection with the assessment of compensation to be paid to the affected persons. The petitioners being in distress consulted their lawyers and on their instructions got the notices served upon the respondents calling upon them to withdraw and rescind the order of requisition. Having not received any reply the petitioners moved this court and obtained the present rule. 

 8. In both the writ petitions it is stated that the self same land was sought to be acquired in L.A. Case No. 122/60-61 and subsequently the L.A. Collector by his notice No. 286 dated 21- 2-1966 announced the de-requisition of the said land whereupon the compensation money paid to the land owners was refunded to the Government and the petitioners were allowed to possess the said land. It is submitted that the area having developed due to the construction of a new road and buildings around, the petitioners have contemplated to build a multi-storied commercial complex upon their respective lands The proposal of certain interested persons offering to buy the land at a nominal price having been turned down they in collusion with the respondents have taken recourse to get the land acquired for their own purpose and personal gain. It is submitted that the scheme of acquiring the land of the petitioners is malafide collusive, arbitrary and has been made in colorable exercise of power by the authority. It is also submitted that the acquisition of land for setting up a 3-Star Hotel cannot be construed as a "public purpose" nor does it meet any of the lawful requirements laid down for acquiring land for public purpose. The acquisition of the land for the purpose of building of 3-Star hotel obviously is not a public purpose nor it is in public interest. For the purpose of establishing a hotel lands could be made available in the city of Dhaka on private negotiation and hence the compulsive acquisition of the petitioners' property is an abuse of the authority as it is not done in the public interest butler the private and commercial gain of some interested person or persons it is further submitted that the original notice under section 3 of the Ordinance was not published in terms of the Ordinance at convenient place on or near the property sought to be acquired. It is further submitted that the initial order being malafide, the subsequent order vide Annexure is also invalid, void and inoperative. 

 9. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 the statements and allegations made in the petition have been controverted. It is stated that the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance Noll of 1982 was duly published on the land under acquisition in L.A. Case No.8/88-89 and also in the notice bard of the Collectorate, Dhaka and other offices on 31-12-88 as required under Rule 4 of the Acquisition of Immovable Property Rules, 1982. It is stated that the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance was duly is sued. The averments made to the effect that the acquisition of land for standard hotels is for a public purpose, as it has been included as one of the service oriented industries in Group-X of the Industrial Investment Schedule for third five years plan (1985-90) for private sector and in order to accelerate the peace of growth of Industries the Government of Bangladesh announced the Industrial Policy in 1986 for the Third five year plan period 1985-90 laying emphasis on private sectors. Two of the objectives are 1) to encourage foreign investment in appropriate sectors, and 2) encourage tourism. The gist of the averment made in the long affidavit sworn by the respondents are that the establishment of the hotel Will pave the way for the investment of foreign capital in our country and in flow of foreign currency of there investment from abroad. The proposed I will serve as a source of encouragement to the tourists and therefore, the acquisition of law for establishing hotel is made for a public purpose and in public interest. The statements and averments made in the affidavit-in-opposition have been also controverted in the affidavit-in-reply filed on behalf of the petitioners. 

 11. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan, the learned counsel for the petitioner after taking us through the petition affidavit-in-opposition.affidavit-in-reply and Annexures challenged the order of requisition on various grounds. Mr. Khan submitted that under Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh every citizen has the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of properly, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalised or requisitioned save by authority of law and this right of the citizen shall be exercised only subject to restrictions which has been imposed under sub-article (2) of the Constitution. Mr. Khan submitted that the law of acquisition as provided under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 empowers the Deputy Commissioner to acquire property under certain conditions when the property is needed or likely to be needed for the public purpose or in the public interest and for that purpose the notice is to be published at convenient place or near the property proposed to be acquired in the prescribed form. But the specific provision of section 3 of the Ordinance has not been adheared to and for such violation the order for acquiring the property of the petitioners is liable to be struck down. By way of elaborating his argument the learned counsel for the petitioners has drawn our attention to Annexure-D' and submitted that the notice was issued under the signature of the land acquisition Officer but the Ordinance provides that the Deputy Commissioner shaft cause the notice to be published. The word Deputy Commissioner as defined under section 2(b) includes an Additional Deputy Commissioner and any other officer authorised by the Deputy Commissioner. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan submitted that there is nothing to show that the land acquisition officer under whose signature the notice is purported to have been issued was duly authorised by the Deputy Commissioner. On perusal of the notice under section 3 it also appears that the land sought to be acquired on the ground that it is necessary for the construction of 3 Star Hotel and also that it is likely to be needed for the construction of the said hotel. Mr. Khan submitted that the property may be needed for the public purpose or it is likely to be needed but while was property the Deputy Commissioner cannot manage to keep both the alternatives in his locket and choose between the two at his pleasure. The use of both the alternatives in the notice under section 3 displays the lack of application of mind of the acquiring authority. 

 "The law of acquisition gives the Deputy Commissioner the power to acquire property in the likelihood of two situations. First, if the property is needed. Or, the property is likely to be needed. A property is either needed or it is likely to be needed. But while acquiring a property the Deputy Commissioner cannot keep both the alternatives in his pocket. He has to choose between the two. If he keeps both the options open, then he does not know whether the property is needed for immediate use or it is likely to be needed for some future use. The use of both these alternative expressions in the notice under section 3 is indicative of a lack of application of mind and the notice under section 3 is liable to be struck down on that ground as well." 

 13. In the instant case the notice issued by the land acquisition officer vide Annexure-D does not speak specifically as to whether the land is needed for immediate use or likely to be needed for future. In view of the principle laid down in the above referred to case we hold that the notice under section 3 suffers from lack of application of mind of the requisitioning authority and for that matter it suffers from legal infirmity 

 14. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan then argued that the notice was not served in the place or near about the property as required under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. The learned Assistant Attorney General also has not been able to show either from the notice or from the record chat the notice was published at any convenient place on or near the property proposed to be acquired. Rule 4(2) of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 also provides that notices under section 3 shall be published at a convenient place or near the property sought to be acquired with copies of such notices displayed in the notice board of the Collectorate. The next point the learned counsel for the petitioners urged is that the purpose for which the property of the petitioners sought to be acquired is neither a public purpose nor it is in the interest of the public. The learned counsel further submits that the purported requisition for the establishment of a 3-Star Hotel at the initiative of a particular person or a group of persons is designed for their pecuniary benefit only and not for public purpose. Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiya, the learned Assistant Attorney General submitted that the establishment of 3-Stars Hotel in Dhaka City will attract the tourist and it will accelerate the flow of foreign exchange to the country from abroad. 

 Public purpose as defined on Willoughby's Constitution of the United States, Volume 3 at page 1740 as quoted in the 15 DLR case is in the following language: 

 18. In the situation as presented in the case, we feel incliend to accept the averments made on behalf of the petitioners that the purpose for which the land sought to be acquired is purely for private benefit and, therefore, placing reliance on the principle laid down in the earlier cases we hold that the contemplated acquisition is not for a public purpose. It has been laid down in several decisions of this Court that the requisitioning authority must "strike a balance between the demand made by the requiring body and the suffering of the expropriated land owner and come to a conclusion of its own after independent application of mind as to the area necessary for the purpose for which the requisition is sought to be made. On a perusal a of the record produced before us, we are of the view that there has been no application of mind of the authority in making the impugned order. As the establishment of 3-Star hotel does not fall within the category of public purpose, we are of the view that the proposed acquisition of the property of the petitioners is not for public purpose, rather it is for the benefit of a group of individuals directly and the benefit of the public or to a section of it is only prospective or remote or incidental. In taking this view we get our support from the principle laid down in the case of Abdus Sobhan Sowdagor and another Versus- Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 14 DLR 486 wherein it is observed:- 

 19. The same principle was laid down in the case reported in 11 DLR at page 222 and 411 wherein it is held that the Government is not empowered to give the property of a private individual to another private individual. The Supreme Court of India in the case reported in AIR 1961 (S.C) 343 laid down the principle that for a decision as to whether the purpose is public purpose or not it is to be seen whether the compensation money is to be paid for acquisition comes from the private individual of public exchequer. Referring to section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance the learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the provision of the said section has not been complied with. In the present case there is no material to show that the person for whom the property was sought to be acquired entered into an agreement with the Government before issuing the notice under section 3 an agreement with the Government and requiring body is sine quo non for the exercise of such power. 

 20. The learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiya, finally opposed the Rule arguing that having regard to the facts that the Divisional Commissioner having made a decision for acquisition of property under section 5(1) considering the reports submitted before him under Section 4(3) about the acquisition of the property such decision of the Divisional Commissioner shall be final and conclusive evidence that the property is needed for a public purpose or in public interest. In this regard the learned Assistant Attorney General referred to the case of Province of East Pakistan -Versus- Dr. Azizul Islam reported in P 1963 (SC) page 296 wherein it was held: 

 21. In the said case the property was requisitioned for the purpose of rehabilitation of displaced person and therefore on the very face of it assumed the character of the public purpose. The learned Assistant Attorney General then referred to the decision reported in 8 DLR(1956) 210 and submitted that whether the property is required for public purpose cannot be questioned in a court of law. With the pas sage of time and change in the law relating to the requisition and acquisition of the property the superior courts have consistently laid down the principle that if the order of requisition and acquisition is made without following the prescribed procedures it is not outside the scope of the superior court to see whether it is for public purpose or for collateral purpose or for the benefit of an individual or a group of individuals. 

 22. In the Case of Md. Mansur Rahman and others -Versus- Province of East Pakistan reported in 14 DLR at page 604 it is found that the purpose for which the acquisition is subject to the scrutiny of the court and the court is entitled to enquire whether the authority seeking to take the property of an individual is required to take it for public purpose or that the purpose for which the land sought to be acquired is at all a public purpose or not. 

 23. In this case there is absolutely no material to show that the public has an interest in the 3-star hotel so as to guarantee that the public benefit will be secured. The 3-star hotel, as it appears from the materials, will be a commercial institution for the purpose of accommodation of the boarders on payment of charges but it can never be for the common benefit of all or a greater number of people and such interest of a few is not sufficient to held that the acquisition is for a public purpose. 

 24. In view of the above, we are of the view that the order for acquiring the property of the petitioners suffers from legal infirmities as the procedure laid down under section 3, 5, 6 and 7 have not been complied with and, therefore, we are unable to accept the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that whatever order has been passed by the authority is deemed to be conclusive. On the contrary we find from the record that there are enough material to show that the purpose for which the property is sought to be acquired is not a public purpose and in that view of the matter we hold that the order for the acquisition of the property as evidenced vide Annexure-'D' and 'F' have been passed without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect.
